chapterBreakdown.gentle: Pressure makes the pattern visible early. A team can work hard, stay disciplined, and still hurt the mission if it leaves adjacent teams exposed. That is why the chapter focuses on silo failure instead of on generic effort problems. The mission is shared, so execution has to be shared too. The chapter's main idea is that teams must cover and move for one another. Support is not a favor here. It is part of how the mission works. When one group helps another group at the point of pressure, the whole effort gets stronger. The chapter also keeps a limit in view. Mutual support does not erase ownership. Teams still need clear standards and clear responsibility, but they must use those responsibilities in ways that protect the larger mission instead of protecting isolated lanes. In Cover and Move, the standard only matters if people can remember it, explain it calmly, and use it before the room gets noisy.
chapterBreakdown.direct: The chapter argues that silos make teams fail even when the people inside those silos are competent. A unit can look strong in its own lane and still damage the mission by leaving adjacent teams unsupported. That is the chapter's pressure point: local success is not real success if the shared objective is breaking around it. Real teams judge success by whether the shared mission can still move. Cover and move means teams act like mutually dependent elements. If one lane is overloaded, delayed, or exposed, the other lanes cannot pretend they are separate. Support is mission logic, not optional generosity. The chapter also draws a firm line against fuzzy accountability. Helping another team does not mean nobody owns anything. It means clear ownership gets used in service of the whole mission rather than as an excuse to ignore the weak point. Cover and Move only works operationally when the team can restate the principle, tie it to one live decision, and name the next supporting move without drifting.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: Pressure strips the talk away fast. Silos make strong groups look productive while the shared objective bleeds out somewhere else. The chapter says that kind of local excellence is fake if it leaves adjacent teams exposed. Cover and move is the answer. Teams have to support one another because every lane depends on the others staying usable. Support is not charity, and it is not soft sentiment. It is how the mission survives pressure. The hard limit stays clear too. Mutual support is not everybody-helping-everybody chaos. Ownership still matters. Standards still matter. The point is to cover the mission together without hiding behind your lane while the whole operation comes apart. The advantage in Cover and Move comes from teams that expose the weak handoff early, kill the excuse fast, and turn the principle into a repeatable move before pressure widens the gap.

chapterBreakdown.gentle: Pressure makes the pattern visible early. Teams can fail even when each subgroup is trying hard. The reason is that effort inside one lane does not automatically protect the whole mission. A team may keep its own work orderly, timely, and impressive while another connected team gets overloaded or stranded. The chapter says that kind of separation is dangerous because shared missions cannot survive long on isolated pockets of competence. That is why the chapter targets silo thinking directly. A siloed team starts acting as if its own responsibilities mark the edge of its concern. Once that happens, people notice only their own scoreboard. They speak as though adjacent breakdowns belong to someone else. The chapter rejects that view because the larger mission does not care where the formal boundary sits. If another team is failing in a way that will damage the shared objective, then your team is already exposed too. The answer the chapter gives is cover and move. Teams have to support one another as mutually dependent elements. The idea is not sentimental. It is operational. When one lane is under pressure, the other lanes help because their own success depends on the weak point recovering. A product team needs support aligned with customer pain. A lab subgroup needs earlier measurements if the next station is going to finish on time. A household or volunteer crew needs people to cover the overloaded role before frustration hardens into blame. The chapter also makes a balancing point. Mutual support does not mean everybody owns everything equally. That would replace silos with confusion. The principle works only when roles stay clear enough for people to know what they owe, where another team is exposed, and how to help without dissolving standards. Support is strongest when ownership is clear. The chapter therefore asks leaders to widen concern without weakening accountability. That is what makes the bridge to the next chapter natural. Once teams stop hiding inside lanes and start supporting each other, they still need plans and communication simple enough to survive pressure. Otherwise interdependence turns messy and fragile instead of strong.
chapterBreakdown.direct: The chapter goes after a structural failure that competent teams excuse too easily. A unit can perform well inside its own lane and still help the mission fail by ignoring adjacent teams. That is the opening claim. Local success is not mission success if the shared objective keeps paying for a broken handoff, an overloaded support point, or a delay that everyone can see but nobody feels responsible to cover. Silo thinking creates that failure. Teams begin treating their formal job boundary as the edge of their concern. They watch their own metrics, protect their own process, and speak as if problems next door belong only next door. The chapter rejects that logic because shared missions produce shared exposure. If another unit is slipping in a way that will damage the overall effort, then your unit is already involved whether you like it or not. That is where cover and move becomes the chapter's central principle. Teams support one another because they are mutually dependent elements, not because support is optional generosity. A support queue and a product backlog are tied together by the same customer pain. A school project's research subgroup and design subgroup are tied together by the same deadline. A household's routines are tied together by the same visible weak point. Once leaders see that, they stop asking only whether their own team is working and start asking where the mission is exposed. The chapter keeps one hard limit visible so the idea does not drift soft. Mutual support is not endless rescue and not fuzzy accountability. Clear ownership still matters. Standards still matter. The point is not that everyone should do everything. The point is that every team should use its own ownership in ways that protect the whole mission instead of using ownership as a reason to ignore the weak point. That is why the chapter has real transfer power. It gives leaders a sharper standard than generic teamwork talk. If your lane looks healthy while the mission around it is failing, then your lane is not healthy enough. Once teams accept that standard, the next challenge appears immediately: how do they keep support strong without making coordination too complicated to execute under pressure?
chapterBreakdown.competitive: Pressure strips the talk away fast. A team can be disciplined, fast, and proud of its lane while the mission as a whole gets weaker. That is the warning. Local excellence becomes a fraud when it leaves adjacent teams overloaded, delayed, or exposed and then pretends those failures belong to somebody else. That is what silo thinking really does. It teaches people to treat the job description as a moral boundary. They watch their own scoreboard, guard their own process, and talk as if breakdowns next door are not their concern. The chapter tears into that posture because shared missions do not respect those comfort lines. If the weak point is elsewhere but the mission will fail because of it, then the weak point is already your business. Cover and move is the answer, and the chapter means it as hard mission logic. Teams support one another because they are mutually dependent elements. One lane does not stay free by pretending the pinned-down lane is separate. One function does not stay strong by watching the other function drown. Product and support share the same customer wound. A lab station waiting on upstream measurements shares the same deadline risk. A family protecting routines while the overloaded chore point keeps collapsing shares the same frustration bill. That is why strong leaders widen their focus. They do not only ask whether their own unit is disciplined. They ask where the mission is bleeding and what support would stop the loss fastest. But the chapter keeps its edge by refusing a soft interpretation. Support is not everybody-helping-everybody chaos. Ownership still matters. Standards still matter. If mutual support erases responsibility, the team has traded silos for disorder. The real standard is sharper than most teams want. Your lane is not successful if it is surviving off someone else's exposure. Your ownership is not clean if you use it to explain away the weak point. Cover and move means protecting the mission together with clear responsibility still intact. That is what sets up the next chapter cleanly. Once teams accept interdependence, they still have to keep plans and communication simple enough not to collapse under the weight of too much coordination.

chapterBreakdown.gentle: The chapter opens by attacking a quiet leadership mistake that often hides behind competence. Teams assume they are doing well because each subgroup is busy, disciplined, and strong inside its own lane. But the chapter says that assumption is dangerous when the mission is shared. A unit can be organized and still fail the whole effort if it leaves connected teams unsupported. That is the opening pressure. The issue is not whether people are trying. The issue is whether they understand that their work lives inside a larger web of dependence. This is why silo thinking matters so much. A siloed team turns formal ownership into the edge of moral concern. People start speaking as if their job is complete when their own metrics are green, even while another team is overloaded, delayed, or exposed in a way that will damage the same mission. The chapter rejects that posture. Shared missions create shared exposure. If the adjacent team is failing in a way that will break the outcome, then the problem is already partly yours whether or not the org chart says so. That is what gives cover and move its real force. The principle does not mean vague supportiveness. It means teams act like mutually dependent elements. One lane helps another because its own success depends on the other lane staying usable. Product and support are tied together by the same customer problem. Upstream research and downstream execution are tied together by the same deadline. Household roles are tied together by the same visible weak point. Once leaders see interdependence that way, support stops looking optional. It becomes part of how the mission survives. The chapter sharpens further when it changes the leader's field of vision. Weak leadership asks whether my team is performing. Stronger leadership asks where the mission is exposed and what support would reduce that exposure fastest. That requires leaders to see across handoffs, dependencies, and weak points instead of only admiring local order. It also requires honesty. Sometimes the next bottleneck is outside your lane but still squarely inside your mission responsibility. The chapter would drift soft if it stopped there, so it preserves a hard limit. Mutual support is not endless rescue. It is not permanent overfunctioning for chronically weak teams. It is not a justification for fuzzy accountability where everybody helps and nobody owns. The principle works only if roles stay clear enough for people to know what they owe and how support should land. Clear ownership lets teams cover one another intelligently. Without that clarity, the team has not built interdependence. It has built confusion. That is why the chapter is stronger than generic teamwork language. It is not saying that people should be nicer or more collaborative in the abstract. It is saying that local excellence becomes strategically false when it survives by letting another part of the mission remain exposed. A team is not really healthy if it needs adjacent teams to absorb all the pressure. A leader is not really protecting standards if those standards become an excuse to ignore the handoff that keeps failing. The transfer value is easy to see because the mechanism repeats across domains. A campus publication can miss quality because writers, editors, and layout each defend their lane while the deadline deteriorates in plain sight. A volunteer crew can resent one another because nobody wants to move resources toward the overloaded task. A family can keep recycling the same arguments because each person protects routine instead of covering the weak point that would calm the whole system.
chapterBreakdown.direct: Pressure exposes the weak point fast. The real standard is not whether each team looks good alone. The standard is whether the shared objective stays protected across connected lanes. Silo thinking breaks that standard fast. Teams start treating formal responsibility as the edge of concern. They watch their own dashboard, guard their own process, and talk as if breakdowns next door belong to somebody else. The chapter rejects that move because shared missions create shared exposure. If another team's delay, overload, or blind spot will damage the outcome, then your team is already in the problem whether the org chart admits it or not. That is why cover and move matters. Teams operate as mutually dependent elements. Support is not optional generosity. It is mission logic. One lane cannot stay healthy by pretending the pinned-down lane is irrelevant. Product does not stay healthy if support is drowning in the same customer pain. A research subgroup does not stay successful if the build subgroup is stalled waiting on measurements. Interdependence means another team's exposure eventually becomes your cost. The chapter also changes what leaders should monitor. Instead of asking only whether their own lane is executing well, leaders have to ask where the mission is exposed and what support would reduce that exposure fastest. That forces leaders to inspect handoffs, dependencies, and shared risk instead of taking comfort in local order. Support the exposed point before local pride convinces you that the weak point belongs to somebody else. But the chapter keeps one hard limit clear. Mutual support does not erase ownership. It is not rescue culture, permanent overfunctioning, or blurred accountability. Clear roles and standards still matter because they tell teams what they owe and how support should land. Without that clarity, cover and move turns into helpful-looking chaos where nobody stays answerable once the rush passes. That limit is what keeps the chapter sharper than generic teamwork rhetoric. Local excellence becomes strategically false when it depends on someone else staying exposed. A clean dashboard can hide a failing mission. A well-run lane can still be a selfish lane. The pattern transfers cleanly because most real systems live on dependencies, from campus publications to volunteer crews to households. Different settings, same rule: the exposed point is already part of your mission. That creates the harder question the chapter leaves open for the next one. How do teams support one another aggressively without building so much coordination overhead that execution collapses under pressure? The answer begins here: keep support tied to mission exposure and clear ownership, then simplify what teams owe one another so the coordination can survive contact with reality. Cover and Move only works operationally when the team can restate the principle, tie it to one live decision, and name the next supporting move without drifting. That is the practical standard here: clear intent, visible support, and immediate correction before confusion compounds.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: Pressure strips the talk away fast. The chapter says that is false. A unit can be fast, disciplined, and proud of its output while the mission gets weaker because adjacent teams are exposed and nobody with real capacity is covering them. That is the opening warning. Local excellence can become camouflage for shared failure. Silos make that lie easier to live with. Once teams start treating the job description as the edge of concern, they watch their own scoreboard and call everything next door somebody else's problem. The chapter tears into that posture because shared missions do not respect those comfort lines. If the weak point will break the outcome, then the weak point is already your business. Pretending otherwise is just a cleaner way to abandon the mission. Cover and move is the corrective, and the chapter means it as hard execution logic. Teams are mutually dependent elements. One lane does not remain healthy by watching the pinned-down lane drown. Product shares the same customer wound as support. The downstream build station shares the same deadline risk as the upstream measurement team. The family member with the easiest routine shares the same stress bill as the person carrying the overloaded chore. Support is not kindness. It is the price of keeping the mission alive. That is why real leaders widen their field of view. They do not ask only whether their own unit looks clean. They ask where the mission is bleeding and what help would stop the loss fastest. They inspect handoffs, delays, overload points, and exposed teams because those are the places where local pride likes to hide. The chapter makes the standard brutal in the right way: if your lane is surviving off someone else's exposure, your lane is not actually strong. But the chapter does not let the principle soften into rescue culture. Mutual support is not endless overfunctioning for weak performers. It is not a feel-good permission slip for blurred accountability. Clear ownership still matters because someone has to remain answerable when the exposed point is named. Standards still matter because help without discipline just spreads confusion across more people. If everybody owns everything, the mission will get sympathy instead of execution. That is what makes the chapter more severe than slogan teamwork. It says local excellence becomes strategically dishonest when it depends on adjacent failure. A polished dashboard can hide a failing mission. A disciplined team can still be a selfish team. A leader can defend standards so narrowly that those standards end up protecting the lane more than the objective. The transfer cases are everywhere. A campus publication misses quality because each subgroup protects its own schedule while the deadline buckles. A volunteer crew breeds resentment because nobody shifts resources toward the overloaded task. A home keeps paying the same stress tax because routines are guarded harder than the weak point is covered. Different setting, same verdict: the exposed point is already inside your responsibility. The chapter's hardest follow-on problem is what keeps it sharp. How do you build aggressive mutual support without turning the whole system into everybody-helping-everybody clutter that collapses under pressure? The answer starts by keeping support ruthless about mission need and equally ruthless about ownership. That is the bridge into the next chapter. Once teams accept interdependence, they still have to simplify plans and communication enough to make that interdependence executable when things get hard.

examples.title: Rina Stops Optimizing the Wrong Win

scenario.gentle: Rina leads a product team during a launch week. The customer support dashboard keeps flashing the same complaint, but Rina is tempted to keep her team focused only on planned feature work so their sprint board still looks clean.
scenario.direct: Rina has to decide whether local productivity matters more than the shared customer problem. The launch is exposing support, and pretending that exposure belongs only to support would leave the mission uncovered.
scenario.competitive: Rina can protect her sprint optics or cover the customer wound hammering support. Only one of those choices actually serves the mission.

whatToDo.gentle: Rina should move engineering help toward the repeated complaint and coordinate directly with support until the weak point is covered.
whatToDo.direct: Treat the overloaded support queue as a product problem too. Shift resources to the shared pain instead of hiding behind the roadmap.
whatToDo.competitive: Cover the bleeding point. If your dashboard stays pretty while support drowns, your lane is fake strong.

whyItMatters.gentle: The chapter says adjacent exposure is already part of your mission when outcomes are shared.
whyItMatters.direct: This shows cover and move clearly: another team's pressure becomes your responsibility when the mission depends on both lanes together.
whyItMatters.competitive: Support is taking fire for the same mission. If Rina will not cover it, she is helping the failure spread.

examples.title: Owen Learns That a Clean Station Can Still Fail the Lab

scenario.gentle: Owen finishes his measurements on time during a lab project and feels good about his section. But the lab station timer keeps running while the next subgroup waits on clarifications Owen never wrote down, and the whole experiment slips.
scenario.direct: The postmortem shows that Owen's local success did not protect the group. His station stayed clean, but the handoff to the next subgroup stayed weak enough to hurt the shared deadline.
scenario.competitive: Owen wants credit for his tidy station, but the lab failed because his lane handed off a problem instead of usable work.

whatToDo.gentle: Owen should rebuild the handoff process so the next subgroup gets what it needs before the timer pressure rises again.
whatToDo.direct: Own the fact that a clean local performance is not enough. The next station needs usable output, not just completed effort.
whatToDo.competitive: Stop grading yourself on your lane alone. If the next team cannot move, you did not really finish.

whyItMatters.gentle: The chapter says shared missions fail when teams care only about their own section of the work.
whyItMatters.direct: This is the anti-silo lesson in school form: the mission is the full experiment, not Owen's narrow checkpoint.
whyItMatters.competitive: A pretty station is worthless if it hands the next station a delay disguised as completion.

examples.title: Jade Stops Guarding Fairness More Than the House

scenario.gentle: Jade keeps repeating that chores should stay exactly divided as planned, even while the shared grocery list grows and one part of the week keeps collapsing under late pickups and meals.
scenario.direct: The conversation sounds like fairness, but the real issue is mission exposure. Jade is protecting role purity while the household weak point keeps taking the hit.
scenario.competitive: Jade keeps defending the contract while the house keeps paying the bill. The lane is protected. The mission is not.

whatToDo.gentle: Jade should ask what weak point needs coverage this week and rebalance effort around the overloaded part of the household.
whatToDo.direct: Shift from defending static roles to covering the exposed point. The goal is a functioning house, not a perfectly frozen split.
whatToDo.competitive: Cover the weak point instead of worshiping the schedule. Fairness that leaves the mission broken is lazy fairness.

whyItMatters.gentle: The chapter shows that support is part of shared success when lives and roles are connected.
whyItMatters.direct: This example makes the principle personal: rigid lane defense can quietly become a form of mission neglect.
whyItMatters.competitive: The household does not care who kept the rulebook clean if dinner and pickup keep exploding.

examples.title: Pavel Speeds Up the Warehouse Only After He Looks Sideways

scenario.gentle: Pavel keeps trying to improve his team's loading speed by tightening only his own checklist. The loading dock pallet map still shows recurring jams at the handoff point with the receiving team, and nothing really improves until Pavel studies that shared choke point.
scenario.direct: The reveal is that Pavel's lane was never the whole problem. Execution improves only when he treats the receiving bottleneck as part of his mission too.
scenario.competitive: Pavel keeps polishing his own station while the real bleed sits one handoff away. The work gets faster only when he finally attacks the shared choke point.

whatToDo.gentle: Pavel should coordinate with the receiving team and adjust his lane based on the shared bottleneck instead of only local speed.
whatToDo.direct: Protect throughput, not lane pride. Once Pavel covers the exposed handoff, the whole operation moves better.
whatToDo.competitive: Stop optimizing the wrong scoreboard. Cover the choke point or keep losing time with nicer spreadsheets.

whyItMatters.gentle: The chapter says real support appears when leaders notice where the mission is actually exposed.
whyItMatters.direct: This example shows that adjacent-team help is often the fastest way to improve your own results too.
whyItMatters.competitive: The warehouse got faster when Pavel stopped pretending the bottleneck belonged to somebody else.

scenario.competitive: Iris can keep her hands clean and miss the issue, or she can get in the room and help the mission survive.

whatToDo.gentle: Iris should help the exposed layout point while keeping responsibilities clear enough that the team learns from the strain.
whatToDo.direct: Cover the deadline-critical weak point, but name ownership clearly so support does not turn into permanent blur.
whatToDo.competitive: Step in hard, then keep accountability sharp. Rescue the issue without pretending roles no longer matter.

whyItMatters.gentle: The chapter says support protects the whole mission when one subgroup is under pressure.
whyItMatters.direct: This example captures the limit too: cover and move means helping the issue ship without dissolving who owns layout long term.
whyItMatters.competitive: The trap is thinking clean role boundaries are more important than a living mission. They are not.

examples.title: Leo Changes the Volunteer Shift Once He Covers the Actual Weak Point

scenario.gentle: Before the change, Leo kept doing his preferred setup task while one check-in table overwhelmed the rest of the event. After the change, he started moving people and supplies toward the overloaded table first, and the whole shift felt calmer.
scenario.direct: The difference was not attitude alone. Leo stopped measuring success by whether his usual lane stayed intact and started measuring it by whether the volunteer mission stayed covered.
scenario.competitive: Before, Leo protected his comfort lane. After, he attacked the weak point. That is why the event finally worked.

whatToDo.gentle: Leo should keep training the crew to notice overload early and shift support toward the exposed point without losing role clarity.
whatToDo.direct: Build the habit of covering the mission's weak spot first, then reset roles once the risk drops.
whatToDo.competitive: Move bodies to the bleed point fast, then reestablish ownership. That is real cover and move.

whyItMatters.gentle: The chapter says support becomes natural once teams stop treating lanes as isolated identities.
whyItMatters.direct: This shows how mutual dependence improves execution when people cover the exposed point instead of protecting routine.
whyItMatters.competitive: The event improved when Leo stopped serving the lane and started serving the mission.

coreSkill.gentle: Learn to notice when a shared mission is being hurt by silo thinking and shift support toward the exposed point.
coreSkill.direct: The core skill is interdependent leadership: cover adjacent teams when the mission is exposed while keeping ownership clear.
coreSkill.competitive: Train yourself to spot where your lane is surviving off someone else's exposure and cover it fast.

plan.gentle: If another team is stuck in a way that will delay our shared outcome, then ask what support from my lane would protect the mission best.
plan.direct: If a cross-functional handoff keeps failing, then treat that weak point as part of my mission instead of as someone else's inconvenience.
plan.competitive: If the next team is taking the hit for the same mission, then stop guarding your lane and cover the bleed.

plan.gentle: If my part of a project looks fine but the group is slipping, then inspect the handoff or overloaded station before praising my own section.
plan.direct: If the deadline risk is forming next door, then help the exposed subgroup while keeping roles clear.
plan.competitive: If the lab or publication is slipping at the handoff, then quit admiring your own station and fix the mission problem.

plan.gentle: If one part of the home or volunteer effort keeps overloading the same person, then rebalance support around that weak point.
plan.direct: If routine fairness is leaving the shared mission exposed, then shift effort toward the real pressure point and name who owns what afterward.
plan.competitive: If the same weak point keeps breaking the house or event, then move help there first and sort the lane map second.

twentyFourHourChallenge.gentle: Within the next day, name one adjacent pressure point that affects your outcome and take one small step to support it.
twentyFourHourChallenge.direct: In the next 24 hours, identify one weak handoff or overloaded role your team has been treating as outside its lane and cover it once on purpose.
twentyFourHourChallenge.competitive: By tomorrow, find one mission bleed your lane has been living off and go cover it.

weeklyPractice.gentle: Once this week, review a shared effort by asking which point was most exposed, not only which role looked busiest.
weeklyPractice.direct: Use one weekly review to inspect adjacent-team strain and decide where support should land before the next pressure spike.
weeklyPractice.competitive: Every week, make your team prove it can see past its own dashboard and cover the next bottleneck.

keyTakeawayCard.competitive: The chapter makes the rule brutal and useful: if you hide behind your lane while the weak point is exposed, you are helping the mission fail.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's main warning about siloed teams?
choices: That silos help teams specialize without any major downside
That local success can still fail the mission when adjacent teams stay unsupported
That support matters only when a team is already weak

explanation.gentle: Yes. The chapter warns that a lane can look strong while the shared mission weakens around it.
explanation.direct: Correct. Local excellence is not enough if the mission is paying for broken handoffs or exposed teams.
explanation.competitive: That answer lands because the chapter is attacking fake strength inside silos, not lack of effort.

questions.prompt: What does cover and move mean in this chapter?
choices: Teams support one another because they are mutually dependent
Leaders should remove all role boundaries when pressure rises
Each team should focus on its own speed and trust the rest to adapt

explanation.gentle: Right. The chapter treats support as part of the mission, not as an extra kindness.
explanation.direct: Exactly. Teams cover one another because shared outcomes depend on connected lanes staying usable.
explanation.competitive: That is the core rule: support is mission logic when the lanes are tied together.

questions.prompt: Why can a team still lose even if it performs well inside its own lane?
choices: Because adjacent breakdowns can still damage the same mission
Because team members should avoid specialization entirely
Because local metrics are never useful

explanation.gentle: Correct. Shared missions can fail when one connected team is left exposed.
explanation.direct: The chapter says local performance does not cancel shared exposure across handoffs and bottlenecks.
explanation.competitive: Your dashboard can stay green while the mission dies one lane over. That is the point.

questions.prompt: In Rina's launch scenario, what is the best application of the chapter?
choices: Keep engineering focused only on its current sprint so the board stays clean
Let support absorb the repeated complaint because that team owns customer tickets
Shift engineering help toward the repeated complaint because support exposure is part of the shared mission

explanation.gentle: Yes. Rina should treat the overloaded support queue as part of the same mission.
explanation.direct: That choice fits the chapter because adjacent-team pressure becomes your problem when outcomes are shared.
explanation.competitive: Cover the customer wound instead of polishing the sprint board. That is real cover and move.

questions.prompt: How does the chapter distinguish mutual support from rescue culture?
choices: Mutual support ignores standards so people can help faster
Mutual support keeps accountability clear while covering the weak point
Mutual support works only when every team does every task

explanation.gentle: Right. The chapter keeps support tied to clear ownership and standards.
explanation.direct: Exactly. Helping another team is not the same as dissolving responsibility or doing everything for them.
explanation.competitive: The chapter refuses rescue fog. Help hard, but keep someone answerable.

questions.prompt: Which choice reflects a common misreading the chapter rejects?
choices: Support is mission logic in a shared effort
Clear ownership makes support stronger
Cover and move means role boundaries no longer matter

explanation.gentle: Yes. The chapter does not erase roles or standards.
explanation.direct: Correct. Mutual support without ownership would turn the principle into confusion.
explanation.competitive: That is the soft drift the chapter blocks. Chaos is not teamwork.

questions.prompt: What is the best transfer of the chapter to a school or volunteer setting?
choices: Protect your own section first because shared effort will balance out later
Cover the overloaded subgroup or task because the whole project depends on it
Wait until the teacher or organizer assigns new roles before helping

explanation.gentle: Correct. The chapter keeps asking people to support the exposed point in a shared mission.
explanation.direct: That answer transfers the anti-silo principle well: help where the deadline or effort is actually exposed.
explanation.competitive: Go where the mission is bleeding, not where your role feels safest.

questions.prompt: In the warehouse scenario, why did Pavel's execution improve only after he looked sideways?
choices: Because his own checklist had been too short
Because the real bottleneck sat at the shared handoff with the receiving team
Because the receiving team stopped making mistakes on its own

explanation.gentle: Yes. Pavel improved the mission by covering the exposed handoff, not by polishing only his own station.
explanation.direct: The chapter pushes leaders to inspect shared choke points because those often decide the outcome.
explanation.competitive: He stopped optimizing the wrong scoreboard and attacked the real bleed point.

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the chapter's deeper synthesis about interdependence and accountability?
choices: Interdependence means every team should blend into one shared role
Interdependence means teams cover exposed adjacent lanes while keeping responsibility clear
Interdependence matters only when a project is already in crisis

explanation.gentle: Right. The chapter joins mutual support and clear ownership instead of treating them as opposites.
explanation.direct: Exactly. Support protects the mission best when teams know both where to help and who remains answerable.
explanation.competitive: That is the hard edge: cover the weak point without letting accountability evaporate.

questions.prompt: How does this chapter set up the next one?
choices: By arguing that interdependence still needs plans and communication simple enough to execute under pressure
By proving that support removes the need for clear planning
By showing that isolated teams should avoid coordination whenever possible

explanation.gentle: Yes. Once teams accept interdependence, they still need simple coordination that can hold up under stress.
explanation.direct: Correct. The chapter bridges forward by saying support alone is not enough if the plan becomes too complex to run.
explanation.competitive: Interdependence without simplicity still breaks. That is why the next chapter has to happen.
